title: Leaping out of the water: Aerial-aquatic locomotion with flapping wings.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded all 11 CSV (comma-separated value) files from the paper's Zenodo deposit (record 19378356, CC-BY-4.0) and counted every line: 289 lines total including headers, i.e. roughly 278 data rows spread over 11 separate small tables. Largest is cost_of_transport_animals.csv at 74 rows; next is flapping_frequency_animals.csv at 36 rows (one row per animal species); the robot-experiment tables hold 9-45 rows each. I read the header and first rows of all 11. The 12th file is a 28 MB Fusion 360 CAD (computer-aided design) archive of the robot, not tabular data.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The abstract only. The paper is paywalled: Europe PMC reports no PubMed Central ID and no open full text, and the author manuscript on MIT DSpace returns HTTP 202 with zero bytes (bot challenge), so I never saw the methods, the figure captions or the data availability statement. The Zenodo link came from a web search quoting the paper's data citation; I confirmed the record exists and matches the title.

a1_downloadable.note: VERIFIED IN FILES: all 11 CSVs download anonymously from Zenodo under CC-BY-4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution). No login, no application. The paper itself is paywalled but the data is not.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: VERIFIED IN FILES: measured outcomes sit in named columns, e.g. 'Lift', 'Drag', 'Power', 'cycle_max_avg' (swim velocity), 'COT' (cost of transport), 'Frq air'/'Frq wat' (flapping frequency in air and water). No construction needed within a single file.

a3_inputs_present.note: VERIFIED IN FILES: the design variables are present as columns (wingspan in mm, flapping frequency in Hz, wind speed, angle of attack, spar diameter, body mass). No identifier lookups required.

a4_units_stated.note: VERIFIED IN FILES: mixed. wing_stiffness.csv and cost_of_transport_animals.csv carry an explicit units row (g, Hz, mm, Pa, J/Nm). The robot force/power tables (wingsize_flight_forces_power.csv, flexibility_flight_forces_power.csv, flexibility_swim_power.csv) have no units row at all — 'Lift', 'Power', 'max_svkg_values' are bare numbers whose units are only recoverable from the paywalled figure captions I could not read.

a5_enough_rows.note: KILLER, VERIFIED BY LINE COUNT: ~278 data rows in total across 11 tables that describe different experiments on different entities (robot configurations versus animal species) and cannot be stacked into one feature/label table. The largest single modellable table is 74 rows; the comparative-biology table is 36 species. The checklist floor is ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification. This is 5-40x short on the whole deposit and ~20x short on any one table.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 35 KB of CSV (the 28 MB CAD file is not needed)
a6_fits_laptop.note: VERIFIED IN FILES: trivially fits. This is the one Part A check the dataset passes comfortably, and it passes because the data is tiny — which is the same fact that kills A5.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: CANNOT VERIFY: the paper is paywalled and the MIT DSpace author manuscript download is blocked, so I had no numbers in the text to compare the 278 rows against. Recorded as unverifiable, not as a disagreement.

a8_label_provenance.note: VERIFIED IN FILES as far as the columns allow: robot rows are physical measurements (force-balance lift/drag, electrical power, video-tracked velocity); the animal rows are literature values with a per-cell citation column naming the source paper (e.g. Lapsansky et al. eLife 2020). No column is another model's output. Note the animal rows are a literature compilation, so the same species may be measured by different labs with different methods.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available: with 74 rows in the largest table and no units on the robot force and power columns, any model fitted here would be describing a handful of experiments, not learning a relationship that generalises.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use wing size, stiffness and flapping rate to predict how much power a flapping robot needs to swim or fly.
plain_idea.train_on: One row per robot configuration or per bird species: wingspan, wing spar diameter (a stand-in for stiffness), flapping frequency, wind speed, tail angle, body mass. I counted the rows myself: ~278 in total across 11 separate tables, the largest single table being 74 rows.
plain_idea.predict: Lift, drag, mechanical power, swimming speed, or cost of transport (energy per unit weight per unit distance). True values come from a laboratory force balance, electrical power logging and video tracking of the 300 g robot in a wind tunnel and a water tank, plus literature values for 36 bird and animal species.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Bio-inspired robotics groups would use a surrogate model to search wing designs without rebuilding the robot, and comparative biomechanists would get a quantitative link between wing shape and the energy cost of moving in two fluids. As designed here it cannot be attempted: there is nowhere near enough data.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: a surrogate model mapping flapping-wing design parameters (span, stiffness, frequency, tail geometry) to aerodynamic and hydrodynamic performance (lift, drag, power, cost of transport), trained on the robot sweeps and calibrated against the 36-species bird comparison. The deposit is figure source data, not a training set — 11 disjoint tables of 9-74 rows each. An interesting salvage, if anyone wanted it, is the 36-species air-versus-water flapping-frequency table joined to AVONET (a public bird morphology database) on Latin name, but 36 species is a scatter plot, not a model.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not estimated: the whole tabular deposit is 35 KB and the 11 files loaded and counted in under a second. Hours-to-table reflects reconciling missing units across files, which I could not complete without the paywalled captions.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: wc -l on the Zenodo CSVs. It took one command and one minute: 289 lines including headers, across 11 tables that do not join. Do this before reading anything else about a robotics or biomechanics paper.

verdict_reason: Part A5 fails decisively and was verified by opening every file: the entire data deposit is ~278 rows spread over 11 unrelated small tables (largest 74 rows), against a floor of ~1,500. This is figure source data for a hardware paper, not a dataset. A4 also fails — the robot lift, drag and power columns carry no units, and the captions that would supply them are behind the Science paywall with the MIT author manuscript download blocked. The data is genuinely open (CC-BY-4.0 on Zenodo) and the measurements are real physical ones, so nothing here is dishonest; there is simply nothing to model. Per the checklist I stopped at the first failed killer and did not score Parts B-J or run the existing-models audit, so the empty c2_audit means 'not searched', not 'nothing exists'.
